title: RBI Rules for Freelancers in India (2026)
summary: RBI rules for freelancers in India cover foreign payments, FEMA compliance, FIRA and taxation. Here's what freelancers must know in October 2026.
body_markdown:
RBI rules for freelancers in India are simple at the core. You do not need RBI permission to work with foreign clients. You only need to receive the money through an authorised dealer (AD) bank, in foreign currency, with the correct purpose code, and keep proof of every payment, such as a FIRA or FIRC.


These rules come under FEMA, and they changed on 1 October 2026. Payments for service exports must now be realised within 9 months of the invoice date, and the older SOFTEX filing has been replaced by the Export Declaration Form (EDF) framework.


This guide explains each rule in plain language, covers the new FEMA changes, and lists every document you need, one by one.


## **TL;DR**


-


**What are the RBI rules for freelancers in India?** Receive payments from foreign clients through an AD bank, in foreign currency, quote the correct purpose code, and keep proof of each payment (FIRA or FIRC). No RBI permission is needed to work with foreign clients.


-


**What changed from 1 October 2026?** RBI’s new FEMA export and import regulations came into force. Service export proceeds must now be realised within 9 months of the invoice date, and the older SOFTEX filing has been replaced by the Export Declaration Form (EDF) framework.


-


**Do freelancers need to report under the new rules?** RBI has clarified that individuals providing services to overseas clients, such as freelancers, need not report under the EDF framework. RBI FAQs are expected to give more detail.


-


**Which documents do freelancers need?** PAN, KYC documents, an AD bank account, a client contract, an export invoice, the purpose code, a FIRA or FIRC, and GST registration with an LUT if you are GST-registered.


-


**How long do you have to receive payment?** 9 months from the invoice date, or 12 months if the export is invoiced or settled in INR.


## **What are the RBI rules for freelancers in India?**


The RBI rules for freelancers in India come down to a short checklist: use an AD bank, get paid in foreign currency, complete KYC, use the correct purpose code, receive the money on time, and keep proof.


**Rule**


**What it means for you**


Use an AD Category-I bank


Foreign payments must reach you through a bank or institution authorised by RBI to deal in foreign exchange.


Get paid in foreign currency


USD, EUR, GBP and other freely convertible currencies are the standard. INR invoicing from foreign clients is possible under specific RBI arrangements.


Complete KYC


Your bank or payment provider verifies who you are before it credits foreign money.


Use the correct purpose code


Every inward remittance carries a code that tells the bank what the payment is for.


Receive the money on time


The full value must be realised within 9 months of the invoice date for services.


Keep proof of every payment


A FIRA or FIRC, along with your invoice and contract, shows the money came from a genuine foreign client.


### **Why do RBI rules apply to your freelance income?**


RBI rules apply because a payment from a foreign client brings foreign currency into India. That movement is governed by the[Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999](https://www.infinityapp.in/blog/fema-compliance-tips-2025-for-exporters-businesses) (FEMA), and RBI administers it.


Your freelance work for a client abroad counts as an export of services. This type of payment is a current account transaction, and these are generally allowed without prior approval from RBI.


The rules are not there to stop you from earning. They exist so that every rupee of foreign income has a clear, traceable record. If you follow the process and keep your paperwork, you have nothing to worry about.


## **What are the new FEMA rules for freelancers from 1 October 2026?**


The Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026 came into force on 1 October 2026 and replaced the earlier export framework. For freelancers, three things matter: the 9-month time limit, the Export Declaration Form (EDF), and RBI’s clarification for individual freelancers.


**What has changed?**


-


The earlier framework has been replaced by one consolidated set of regulations for exports and imports of goods and services.


-


Authorised dealer banks now play a bigger role in reporting service exports.


-


The older SOFTEX filing for software and IT service exports has been replaced by the EDF framework.


-


RBI amended the regulations on 22 September 2026, before they started, and set the realisation period for service exports at 9 months from the invoice date. Many older articles still say 15 months.


### **What is the Export Declaration Form (EDF)?**


The EDF is a declaration of the value of services exported to customers outside India. It is filed through your AD bank. The rules allow one monthly declaration that covers services provided to one or more overseas clients during that month.


### **Do freelancers need to file an EDF?**


Individual freelancers do not need to report under the EDF framework, according to RBI’s clarification. RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said that individuals undertaking transactions of a personal nature need not report them. A report dated 8 October 2026 adds that individuals who serve overseas clients, such as online tutors or small software service providers, are not required to report under the EDF rules, whatever the amount.


The position can be different if you operate as an agency or a business. Reports say exporters can use a simpler self-declaration route for bills up to Rs 10 lakh each. RBI has also said that FAQs will be issued soon. Until they are out, confirm your own case with your AD bank or payment provider.


*Read more:*[Export Declaration Form (EDF): Rules, Deadlines & EDPMS (2026)](https://www.infinityapp.in/blog/export-declaration-form)


**What should you do now?**


1.


Note the invoice date of every foreign client invoice, because the 9-month clock starts from it.


2.


Ask your bank or payment provider whether any EDF reporting applies to your type of freelance work.


3.


Collect a FIRA or FIRC for every payment.


4.


Keep your invoices, contracts and purpose codes in one folder.


## **Which documents do freelancers need to receive foreign payments?**


Freelancers need a PAN, KYC documents, an AD bank account, a client contract, an export invoice, the correct purpose code and a FIRA or FIRC. GST documents apply only if you are GST-registered, and the EDF applies only if your bank says it does.


Here is the checklist at a glance.


**Document**


**Why you need it**


**Who provides it**


PAN card


Identifies you for banking and tax


Income Tax Department


KYC documents


Verifies identity and address


You, to your bank or provider


AD bank account


Receives the foreign payment


AD Category-I bank or authorised provider


Client contract


Shows the nature of the work


You and your client


Export invoice


Links the payment to a service


You


Purpose code


Tells the bank what the payment is for


You, from the RBI list


FIRA or FIRC


Proof of inward remittance


Your bank or payment provider


GST registration and LUT


For zero-rated exports, if registered


GST portal

Declaration of service exports, if applicable


Filed through your AD bank

### **1. PAN card**


**What it is:** Your Permanent Account Number, issued by the Income Tax Department.


**Why you need it:** Banks and payment providers need it to verify you and to report foreign income correctly. It also goes on your invoices.


**Where to get it:** Apply on the Income Tax e-filing portal if you do not have one.


### **2. KYC documents**


**What they are:** Identity and address proof, such as Aadhaar, passport, voter ID or driving licence.


**Why you need them:** Know Your Customer checks are mandatory before a bank or provider credits foreign money. They help prevent fraud and money laundering.


**Where to get them:** You already hold these. Your bank or provider will ask for copies or a digital verification.


### **3. An account with an AD Category-I bank**


**What it is:** A bank account with a bank, or a provider, authorised by RBI to deal in foreign exchange.


**Why you need it:** All foreign payments must come through an authorised channel. This is the core RBI rule.


**Where to get it:** Open one with your bank, or onboard with an RBI-regulated platform. Infinity is AD-1 certified and RBI-regulated, and onboarding takes about 2 minutes, with KYC completed the same day.


### **4. Client contract or statement of work**


**What it is:** A written agreement that names you, your client, the service, the fee and the payment terms.


**Why you need it:** It is the strongest proof that the payment is for genuine work. Not every bank asks for it, but you should have it ready.


**Where to get it:** Draft it with your client. Even a simple email agreement or statement of work helps.


### **5. Export invoice**


**What it is:** The bill you send to your foreign client.


**Why you need it:** It links the payment to a service, and its date starts the 9-month realisation clock.


**What it should include:** Your name and address, your PAN (and GSTIN if registered), the client’s name and address, invoice number and date, a clear description of the service, the amount and currency, and payment terms.


### **6. Purpose code**


**What it is:** An RBI code that states the nature of the payment.


**Why you need it:** Every inward remittance carries one. A wrong code can cause delays or questions from the bank.


**Where to get it:** From the RBI purpose code list.[Infinity’s purpose code finder](https://tools.infinityapp.in/purpose-code) helps you pick the right one. See the next section for how to choose.


### **7. FIRA or FIRC**


**What it is:** A Foreign Inward Remittance Advice (FIRA) or Foreign Inward Remittance Certificate (FIRC) is proof that a specific foreign payment reached you. It shows the remitter, amount, currency and purpose.


**Why you need it:** It is your main proof of a compliant payment. You will need it at tax time, for GST export documentation and in any reconciliation.


**Where to get it:** From your bank or payment provider. Infinity generates a FIRA automatically for your payments at no extra cost.


*Read more:*[FIRA vs FIRC guide](https://www.infinityapp.in/blog/fira-vs-firc)


### **8. GST registration and LUT (if applicable)**


**What it is:** If you are GST-registered, you can export services without paying GST by filing a[Letter of Undertaking (LUT)](https://www.infinityapp.in/blog/download-the-lut-certificate-in-gst) .


**Why you need it:** Export of services is zero-rated under GST. Registration is generally needed only when your turnover crosses the GST threshold, which is Rs 20 lakh in most states.


**Where to get it:** Register and file the LUT on the GST portal.


### **9. Export Declaration Form (EDF), if applicable**


**What it is:** The monthly declaration of services exported, filed through your AD bank.


**Why you need it:** It applies to service exporters under the new FEMA rules. As covered above, RBI has clarified that individual freelancers need not report.


**Where to get it:** Through your AD bank. Check with them whether it applies to you.


### **10. Proof of work delivered**


**What it is:** Emails, delivery confirmations, approvals or shared files that show you completed the work.


**Why you need it:** It supports your invoice if the bank or an auditor asks questions later.


**Where to get it:** Save these as you work.


### **Documents freelancers usually do not need**


Freelancers often worry about forms that mostly apply to other situations. If you are an individual freelancer receiving payments from foreign clients, you will usually not need the three documents below. Your bank or payment provider can confirm if your case is different.


**Form 15CA and 15CB: usually not needed.**


[Form 15CA and 15CB](https://www.infinityapp.in/blog/form-15ca-15cb-tax-rules-for-sending-money-abroad) are mainly for money going out of India, such as payments to foreign vendors. Freelance income coming in is the opposite direction, so they generally do not apply to you.


**SOFTEX: not needed from 1 October 2026.**


[SOFTEX](https://www.infinityapp.in/blog/softex-for-indian-exporters) was the form used to declare software and IT service exports. It has been replaced by the Export Declaration Form (EDF) framework. As covered earlier, RBI has clarified that individual freelancers need not report under the EDF framework.


**Import Export Code (IEC): usually not needed for services.**


An[IEC](https://www.infinityapp.in/blog/iec-code-in-india-what-it-is-who-needs-it-how-to-apply) is generally not required to receive payments for services. It matters mainly if you want to claim specific export incentives. If you are unsure, confirm with a professional before applying.


If your situation is unusual, for example if you run an agency or a registered business, check with your bank before assuming you can skip any of these.
